title: AC-flux-driven SQUID diode spectroscopy as a probe of current-phase relations
authors: Yuriy Yerin, Iman Askerzade, Alexey Fedorchenko, Ali Gencer, Oleksandr Dobrovolskiy
abstract: The current-phase relation (CPR) of a Josephson junction encodes microscopic information on superconducting states through higher-order and fractional harmonics. However, their unambiguous extraction is challenging, as different CPR components produce nearly identical static interference patterns that are further obscured by device asymmetries, damping, and dynamical effects. Here, we propose probing individual CPR harmonics via the ac magnetic-flux-driven diode effect in asymmetric dc SQUIDs with unequal junction critical currents. Using two complementary reductions of the fast-driven dynamics -- a Kapitza-type perturbation theory for the conventional junction and a Jacobi--Anger averaging for a general CPR -- we show that ac flux modulation dresses each harmonic with a distinct Bessel function, yielding characteristic signatures in the diode efficiency $η(φ_{\rm ac},ω)$ as a function of ac flux amplitude $φ_{\rm ac}$ and frequency $ω$. We verify and extend these predictions by numerical solutions of the coupled dynamical equations for CPRs containing $\sin\varphi$, $\sin(\varphi/2)$, and $\sin 2\varphi$ terms ($\varphi$: superconducting phase difference), and construct phase diagrams of $η(φ_{\rm ac},ω)$. Distinct CPR components are revealed to produce characteristic weak, sparse, dense, or intermodulated arc patterns that remain robust in both overdamped and underdamped regimes. This suggests ac-flux-driven SQUID diode spectroscopy as a probe of current-phase relations in topological materials, multiband systems, and other unconventional superconductors.
summary: This work proposes using AC magnetic-flux-driven SQUID diode spectroscopy as a novel diagnostic tool for mapping the Current-Phase Relation (CPR) in unconventional superconductors. By analyzing the resulting 2D phase diagram of the diode efficiency, researchers can distinguish between different CPR harmonics ($\sin\phi$, $\sin(\phi/2)$, $\sin(2\phi)$) based on characteristic Bessel function patterns. This method offers a robust way to probe exotic superconducting states like those found in topological or multiband materials.
main_problem: The primary challenge is unambiguously extracting individual Current-Phase Relation (CPR) harmonics from the CPR spectrum, as different components yield nearly identical static interference patterns obscured by device asymmetries and dynamics.
main_result: AC magnetic-flux-driven SQUID diode spectroscopy provides a high-resolution diagnostic tool, revealing distinct fingerprints of various CPR harmonics ($\sin\phi$, $\sin(\phi/2)$, $\sin(2\phi)$) through characteristic Bessel function dressings in the 2D phase diagram $\eta(\varphi_{ac}, \omega)$.
method: The authors use complementary reductions of fast-driven dynamics, including Kapitza-type perturbation theory and Jacobi–Anger averaging, to analyze the diode efficiency $\eta$ as a function of AC flux amplitude ($\varphi_{ac}$) and frequency ($\omega$).
model_or_system: The system is an asymmetric DC SQUID with unequal junction critical currents. The model incorporates Josephson junctions whose CPRs can contain higher-order or fractional harmonics, such as $\sin(\phi/2)$ (4$\pi$-periodic) and $\sin(2\phi)$ ($\pi$-periodic).
key_observables: Diode efficiency $\eta(\varphi_{ac}, \omega)$, which exhibits characteristic nodal line patterns governed by Bessel functions ($J_0(\xi_0)$, $J_0(\xi_0/2)$, $J_0(2\xi_0)$).
important_parameters: AC flux amplitude ($\varphi_{ac}$), driving frequency ($\omega$), and the damping regime (overdamped to underdamped).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations like assuming $ eta_L \ll 1$ for Jacobi-Anger reduction, and that the system dynamics can be mapped onto an effective CPR structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate static ($\eta(\varphi_{dc})$), frequency ($\eta(\omega)$), and full 2D phase diagrams ($\eta(\varphi_{ac}, \omega)$) showing distinct arc patterns corresponding to different underlying CPR harmonics.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theoretical framework by first establishing the SQUID model, then applying fast-averaging techniques (Jacobi-Anger), and finally mapping the resulting effective CPR components onto measurable signatures in the 2D phase diagram $\eta(\varphi_{ac}, \omega)$ for various harmonic content.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful, non-invasive transport measurement to probe microscopic quantum details of superconducting order parameters (like fractional or higher harmonics) that are otherwise difficult to measure directly.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the asymmetric dc SQUID geome- try. The device consists of two Josephson junctions (1 and 2) threaded by an external magnetic flux Φe = Φdc + Φac cosωt, with dc and ac flux components and biased by the dc current Ib. Junction 1 is a conventional junction with a purely sinusoidal CPR, while junction 2 may support subharmonic and second- harmonic contributions, as described by Eq. (7).

FIG. 2. Diode efficiency η(φdc,α) of a dc SQUID with two purely sinusoidal Josephson junctions for βc = 1 and βL = 0.15 in the static regime (φac = 0). The cross marks the working point (φdc = 0.25, α = 0.7) used in the remainder of this work.

FIG. 3. Static diode efficiency η(φdc) at φac = 0, βc = 1, βL = 0.15, and α = 0.7, for the four CPR cases defined by Eq. (7), as indicated in the legend. The dotted black curve shows the analytical prediction from Eq. (14). Vertical dotted lines mark the time-reversal symmetric flux values φdc = 0 and φdc = ±1/2.

FIG. 4. Frequency dependence of the diode efficiency η(ω) at fixed φac = 1.5, φdc = 0.25, βc = 1, βL = 0.15, and α = 0.7, for the four CPR cases, as indicated. The dotted black curve shows the analytical prediction from Eq. (15).

FIG. 5. Flux-drive-amplitude dependence of the diode efficiency η(φac) at φdc = 0.25, βc = 1, βL = 0.15, and α = 0.7 for four CPR cases: (a) pure amplitude asymmetry, (b) subharmonic only, (c) second-harmonic only, and (d) mixed harmonics. Each panel shows two curves corresponding to ω = 1 (solid blue with markers) and the adiabatic limit ω = 7.5 (dotted red).
